description:
A one minute sample of an 18 minute stereo recording. The general sound of the wetland marsh that night, mostly dominated by the banjo-like "twang" call of the Green Frogs. There is no adjustment of volume levels. There are an interesting variety of frog sounds, often quite close to the microphone, and in a beautiful stereo landscape of evening insects, with only the faint murmer of the nearby natural gas compressor station. 

The background meadow and wetland insects are as interesting as the frogs of course, as well as a number of geat incidental sounds such as frogs plopping about in the water right in front of the microphone. Very evocotive of the night time cattail marsh environment! 

Recorded with a RØDE Stereo Videomic Pro microphone mounted on a Canon EOS Rebel T3i camera shooting video. This microphone is able to overcome the noise of the camera's pre-amp to produce this superb quality digital audio. Try listening to this with headphones!

description:
I saw several of these medium size frogs (head & body length I would estimate around 6 centimeters, or 2 1/4 inches), but they were all in the water, and being elusive, and variously concealed by floating Common Duckweed. The third of them was a little more visible, revealing the dorso-lateral ridges or skin folds down their sides that distinguish the Green Grog from the similar looking Bull Frog. 

They also sound quite different when calling, but I heard no frogs that mostly cloudy day in late May. Perhaps I will stop back with my audio recording gear some warm evening a little later in the year. 

This was in a patch of shallow open water in a cattail marsh constructed along Little Daniels Creek in State Game Lands #297. I am always thrilled to see vertebrates especially in such environments, because they are usually so good at remaining hidden. I will return hoping to find perhaps some snakes, turtles, even Muskrats. Something is chewing on a few cattail stalks here! 

[I returned on 10 July, 2023 and didn't hear frogs at this precise location, but recorded both Green Frogs and Cope's Gray Treefrogs *Hyla chrysoscelis* (!) in similar marshes in the same State Gamelands just over one kilometer to the north. 
See:
